title: You cannot copy individuality: Hawkins-inspired tenors
summary: Every player copies someone but ends with his own character. He sorts Herschel Evans, Byas, Webster, Lucky Thompson and others as Hawkins players, with Getz, Zoot and Bud Johnson from the other camp.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: As a reed player, of course, you played with and heard all the great reed players from an era when there were so many, and we were talking before about how each one was a great individual even if he was working in a style. Of course, Hawkins was the man who really brought the tenor saxophone out front, and people were influenced by him. But they -- but all of them had their own --

Well, as they tell you, you know, the only thing about copying, you can't copy individuality. The two -- everyone has played or were inspired to play like someone, and I think that everybody that played an instrument copied someone. But not -- but the same thing didn't come out

eventually because there's a certain individual thing that God gave everybody that's different from everybody else. And you can't -- you just can't copy it. You can get the idea, but you can't -- you can always tell the difference between the real thing and something else, and the other thing always develops into another complete style or another complete character.
You were mentioning about Ben Webster and Don Byas and --
-- Herschel Evans came out of Hawkins too, didn't he?

That's right, Herschel Evans, Don -- Lucky Thompson, Don Byas, Ben Webster, Lockjaw Davis. All of those were -- Hawk inspired players -- Ike Quebec. And then you turn around on the other hand and you'll find guys like Bud Johnson, Stan Getz, Zoot Simms and all of them were -- Zoot was half in between.
Well, he liked Ben too. He always said that.
Well, he -- Zoot is between them, but all of these things are -- developed into another character altogether.
